ch15_ex1_q1: Memory pattern: $\sin(0^\circ), \sin(30^\circ), \sin(45^\circ), \sin(60^\circ), \sin(90^\circ)$ are $\frac{\sqrt{0}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{1}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{4}}{2}$. Cosine runs the same list backwards.
Complementary link: $\sin(30^\circ) = \cos(60^\circ)$, because the side opposite $30^\circ$ is the side adjacent to $60^\circ$.
ch15_ex1_q2: Set up the sine rule with the unknown side on top ($\frac{x}{\sin(60^\circ)} = \frac{7}{\sin(42^\circ)}$) so a single multiplication finishes the job.
Estimate: $\sin(60^\circ) \approx 0.87$ and $\sin(42^\circ) \approx 0.67$, a ratio of about 1.3, so $x \approx 7 \times 1.3 \approx 9.1$.
ch15_ex1_q3: The ratio $\frac{\text{side}}{\sin(\text{opposite angle})}$ is the same for all three pairs. Here $\frac{10}{\sin(55^\circ)} \approx 12.21$; store it, then any side is this number times the sine of its opposite angle.
Angles $50^\circ$ and $55^\circ$ are close, so their opposite sides should be close too: $y$ just under 10 is the right size.
ch15_ex1_q4: Why $B' = 180^\circ - B$: triangle $BCB'$ is isosceles ($CB = CB'$), so its base angles are equal, and the angle $AB'C$ is supplementary to the base angle at $B'$.
Two triangles appear when the side opposite the given angle (11) is shorter than the other given side (19) but longer than the height $19\sin(25^\circ) \approx 8.03$.
ch15_ex1_q5: Quick ambiguity test: the given angle $63^\circ$ is opposite the longer given side (7 > 5), so only one triangle is possible.
The side opposite the largest angle ($C \approx 77^\circ$) must be the longest side, so $x$ should beat 7. It does.
ch15_ex1_q6: The cosine rule is Pythagoras with a correction: at $90^\circ$, $x = \sqrt{244} \approx 15.6$. An acute angle like $37^\circ$ subtracts a positive amount, so $x$ must be shorter than 15.6.
By the triangle inequality, $x$ must lie between $12 - 10 = 2$ and $22$; use this to catch a slip.
ch15_ex1_q7: Estimate before choosing: $\sin(55^\circ) \approx 0.8$, so the area is about $0.8 \times 22.75 \approx 18.2$, which points straight to B.
Why the formula works: $6.5\sin(55^\circ)$ is the perpendicular height onto the 7 cm side, so it is just $\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$.
ch15_ex1_q8: The reference angle in the third quadrant is $203^\circ - 180^\circ = 23^\circ$; there sine and cosine are both negative and tangent is positive.
ch15_ex1_q9: Why it is exactly 0.5: the origin, $(1, 0)$ and the point at $60^\circ$ form an equilateral triangle of side 1, so the perpendicular from P lands at the midpoint $x = \frac{1}{2}$.
ch15_ex1_q10: Picture a right triangle with hypotenuse 1 and adjacent side $p$; Pythagoras makes the opposite side $\sqrt{1 - p^2}$.
Test a value to eliminate options: with $x = 60^\circ$, $p = 0.5$ and $\sin(120^\circ) \approx 0.866 = \sqrt{0.75}$. Only D matches.
ch15_ex1_q11: Memory aid: the number in front stretches the graph up and down (amplitude); the number inside squashes it sideways, giving $n$ full cycles every $360^\circ$.
ch15_ex1_q12: Fast elimination: substitute $x = 0$. Options C and D give 0, A gives 4, and only B gives $-4$.
Count peaks: two maxima between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ means two cycles, so the number inside is 2.
ch15_ex1_q13: The sine graph is symmetric about $x = 90^\circ$, so the two solutions in $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$ always add to $180^\circ$: $30^\circ + 150^\circ = 180^\circ$.
Option B is a trap: $\sin(210^\circ)$ is negative because $210^\circ$ is in the third quadrant.
ch15_ex1_q14: Doubling the angle doubles the number of cycles, so expect 4 solutions in $0^\circ$ to $360^\circ$ instead of the usual 2.
Check an option by substitution: $x = 67.5^\circ$ gives $\cos(135^\circ) = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, which is correct.
ch15_ex1_q15: $\sin(x) = 1$ and $\sin(x) = -1$ are special: they hit only the top or bottom of the wave, so each has just one solution per $360^\circ$ cycle.
Link: $y = 7\sin(x)$ has amplitude 7, so $-7$ is its minimum value, which occurs at $270^\circ$.
